questionText:
For the given sets $A$ and $B$, complete the given diagram.
i. An onto (surjective) function from $A$ to $B$ (1 Mark)
ii. An into function from $B$ to $A$ (1 Mark)
iii. Can we write an onto function from $B$ to $A$? Justify with a reason. (1 Mark)
modelAnswer:
i. Map all elements of $A = \{a, b, c, d\}$ to $B = \{1, 2, 3\}$ such that every element in $B$ has at least one pre-image (e.g., $a \to 1, b \to 2, c \to 3, d \to 3$).
ii. Map elements of $B = \{1, 2, 3\}$ to $A = \{a, b, c, d\}$ such that the range is a proper subset of $A$ (e.g., $1 \to a, 2 \to b, 3 \to c$, leaving $d$ unmapped).
iii. No, an onto function from $B$ to $A$ cannot be constructed because $n(B) = 3$ is strictly less than $n(A) = 4$. For an onto function, the domain must have at least as many elements as the codomain.

questionText: Find the continued product of the expression $(1 - 2a)(1 - 2a + 4a^2)(1 + 2a)(1 + 2a + 4a^2)$.
modelAnswer:
Rearrange terms to pair factors according to the sum and difference of cubes formulae:
$[(1 - 2a)(1 + 2a + 4a^2)] \times [(1 + 2a)(1 - 2a + 4a^2)]$
$= [1^3 - (2a)^3] \times [1^3 + (2a)^3]$
$= (1 - 8a^3)(1 + 8a^3)$
Applying $(x - y)(x + y) = x^2 - y^2$:
$= 1^2 - (8a^3)^2 = 1 - 64a^6$.

questionText: If $x = 2 - \sqrt{3}$, then find the value of $x + \frac{1}{x}$ in the simplest form.
modelAnswer:
Find the reciprocal of $x$ and rationalise the denominator:
$\frac{1}{x} = \frac{1}{2 - \sqrt{3}} \times \frac{2 + \sqrt{3}}{2 + \sqrt{3}} = \frac{2 + \sqrt{3}}{2^2 - (\sqrt{3})^2} = \frac{2 + \sqrt{3}}{4 - 3} = 2 + \sqrt{3}$.
Then add $x$ and $1/x$:
$x + \frac{1}{x} = (2 - \sqrt{3}) + (2 + \sqrt{3}) = 4$.

questionText: Find the possible values of $p$, if $(px - p)$ is divided by $\left(x - \frac{4}{p}\right)$ and the remainder is $p^2 - p$.
modelAnswer:
By the Remainder Theorem, substitute $x = \frac{4}{p}$ into $P(x) = px - p$:
Remainder $= p\left(\frac{4}{p}\right) - p = 4 - p$.
Equate to given remainder: $4 - p = p^2 - p \implies 4 = p^2 \implies p^2 = 4 \implies p = \pm 2$.

solve the expression to find the remainder using remainder theorem;
(Note: when a polynomial of degree up to 4 is divided by polynomial of degree up to 2)

mappingReason:
By the Remainder Theorem, substitute $x = \frac{4}{p}$ into $P(x) = px - p$:
Remainder $= p\left(\frac{4}{p}\right) - p = 4 - p$.
Equate to given remainder: $4 - p = p^2 - p \implies 4 = p^2 \implies p^2 = 4 \implies p = \pm 2$.

questionText: If $a : b :: c : d$, then show that $\frac{5a - 3b}{5a + 3b} = \frac{5c - 3d}{5c + 3d}$ by using K-method.
modelAnswer:
Let $\frac{a}{b} = \frac{c}{d} = k \implies a = bk$ and $c = dk$.
LHS $= \frac{5(bk) - 3b}{5(bk) + 3b} = \frac{b(5k - 3)}{b(5k + 3)} = \frac{5k - 3}{5k + 3}$.
RHS $= \frac{5(dk) - 3d}{5(dk) + 3d} = \frac{d(5k - 3)}{d(5k + 3)} = \frac{5k - 3}{5k + 3}$.
Since $\text{LHS} = \text{RHS} = \frac{5k-3}{5k+3}$, the equality is proved. (Historical curriculum topic; no direct outcome in current IX-X syllabus).

questionText: If $A = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}$, then verify that $(AB)^{-1} = B^{-1} \times A^{-1}$.
modelAnswer:
$AB = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}$.
$\det(AB) = 1(1) - 2(0) = 1$. $\text{adj}(AB) = \begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}$, so $(AB)^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}$.
Since $B = I$, $B^{-1} = I = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}$.
$\det(A) = 1$, $A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}$.
$B^{-1} \times A^{-1} = I \times A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}$.
Therefore $(AB)^{-1} = B^{-1} \times A^{-1}$. (Matrices have moved to current Grade X).

questionText:
In the given diagram, $ABCD$ is a parallelogram and the side $BC$ of the parallelogram is passing through the midpoints $AE$ and $ED$ of the triangle $AED$.
Find the length of
i. $AD$ (1 Mark)
ii. $BE$ (1 Mark)
iii. $CF$ (1 Mark)
modelAnswer:
In $\Delta AED$, $B$ is the midpoint of $AE$ and $F$ is the midpoint of $ED$.
By the Midpoint Theorem, $BF = \frac{1}{2}AD$. The diagram gives $BF = 5\text{ cm} + 5\text{ cm} = 10\text{ cm}$, or $BC = BF + FC = 5 + 5 = 10\text{ cm}$.
In parallelogram $ABCD$, opposite sides are equal: $AD = BC = 10\text{ cm}$.
ii. Since $B$ is the midpoint of $AE$ and $AB = 5\text{ cm}$ (opposite side $CD = 5\text{ cm}$), $BE = AB = 5\text{ cm}$.
iii. Side $BC$ passes through midpoints, giving $CF = 5\text{ cm}$ (or $FD = 6\text{ cm} \implies EF = 6\text{ cm}$).

questionText:
Sarah was playing with a thread connecting to pins on a soft board. The positions of the pins were labelled as $U$, $V$, $W$ and $X$.
She measured the threads connecting the pins as $VW = 7\text{ cm}$, $UX = 4\text{ cm}$ and $WY = 3\text{ cm}$.
She observed that the angles $UVX$ and $WVX$ were equal in measurement and the thread $XV$ bisected the thread connected to $UW$ at right angle.
Based on the given information,
i. find the length of the threads connecting $U$ and $V$. (1 Mark)
ii. find the length of the threads connecting $W$ and $X$. (1 Mark)
iii. what would be the minimum length of thread required to connect $U$ and $W$? (1 Mark)
modelAnswer:
i. Since $XV$ is the angle bisector and right bisector of $UW$, $\Delta UVX \cong \Delta WVX$. Therefore $UV = VW = 7\text{ cm}$.
ii. Any point on the right bisector is equidistant from the endpoints: $WX = UX = 4\text{ cm}$.
iii. The line segment $UW$ is perpendicular to $XV$ at $Y$, and $Y$ is the midpoint of $UW$. Since $WY = 3\text{ cm}$, the full straight thread length $UW = 2 \times WY = 2 \times 3 = 6\text{ cm}$. (Shortest distance between two points is the straight line segment).

d. equidistant from two given intersecting straight lines;

mappingReason:
i. Since $XV$ is the angle bisector and right bisector of $UW$, $\Delta UVX \cong \Delta WVX$. Therefore $UV = VW = 7\text{ cm}$.
ii. Any point on the right bisector is equidistant from the endpoints: $WX = UX = 4\text{ cm}$.
iii. The line segment $UW$ is perpendicular to $XV$ at $Y$, and $Y$ is the midpoint of $UW$. Since $WY = 3\text{ cm}$, the full straight thread length $UW = 2 \times WY = 2 \times 3 = 6\text{ cm}$. (Shortest distance between two points is the straight line segment).

questionText:
In the given diagram, $AE = 9\text{ cm}$, $EC = 6\text{ cm}$, $DE = 12\text{ cm}$ and $BC = 20\text{ cm}$.
Prove that the triangles $ADE$ and $ABC$ are similar.
modelAnswer:
Calculate the total length of side $AC = AE + EC = 9 + 6 = 15\text{ cm}$.
Compute the ratio of corresponding sides:
$\frac{AE}{AC} = \frac{9}{15} = \frac{3}{5}$.
$\frac{DE}{BC} = \frac{12}{20} = \frac{3}{5}$.
Both triangles share the common angle $\angle A$ (or $\angle DAE = \angle BAC$).
Since the ratios of corresponding sides are equal ($\frac{AE}{AC} = \frac{DE}{BC} = \frac{3}{5}$) and the included angle is congruent, $\Delta ADE \sim \Delta ABC$ by SAS similarity (or SSS similarity of corresponding sides).
